fullText:
Suit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information

McDonald’s is facing a lawsuit in federal court over its alleged use of an AI tool to determine pricing across independent franchises, which prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for Americans.

The vast majority of McDonald’s US stores are independently owned and are said to individually decide on prices under company policy. Antitrust laws require businesses to set prices independently from their competitors, as coordinating prices can stifle market competition and push up costs for consumers.

The lawsuit, filed on 2 October in a federal Chicago courtroom, alleges that McDonald’s AI tool is illegal because it amounts to independent franchise locations exchanging nonpublic price and sales data.

“This case is about McDonald’s bringing ‘optimization’ to America’s largest fast food chain,” the complaint says. “McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of US restaurants. The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.”

In response to the lawsuit, a spokesperson for the McDonald’s corporation said that the “complaint is filled with inaccuracies and we will vigorously defend against this lawsuit”.

“AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do,” it said. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.”

A recent Reuters investigation reported that some McDonald’s franchise owners have been pressured by the company to use the AI pricing tools and record their deviations from the tool’s recommendations. McDonald’s contested that characterization, calling the Reuters reporting “speculative and uninformed”.

The litigation, which has been proposed as a nationwide class-action lawsuit, was first brought forward by an Illinois man named Michael Thomas. Thomas, a McDonald’s regular who is described as “price conscious”, found that the cost of his usual order – a Quarter Pounder with cheese, fries and a Coke – varied even within his neighborhood in DeKalb, Illinois. The attorney listed as representing Thomas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Thomas does not appear to be alone in his experience. At a McDonald’s in Manhattan’s financial district, Chukwama Okeke, 43, was finishing a mango-pineapple smoothie that he bought as part of a value meal that cost about $15 – something he only gets about once a month.

Okeke said that when he orders the same meal at a McDonald’s in Brooklyn’s Crown Heights neighborhood, he ends up paying closer to $9.

“McDonald’s in Manhattan is much more expensive than those in Brooklyn,” he said. “I’ve notice in some areas if they have a lot of like foot traffic, the prices tend to get higher.”

Beatriz Milander, 27, who ordered a snack wrap, a small fries and an iced coffee for $11.51, hadn’t noticed a huge difference between what she pays in the financial district and what she pays in her Bronx neighborhood, but said prices overall had inched up.

“In the last few months, I’ve seen them do more deals or like lower-priced things,” she said. “But it definitely was pricing up for a little bit there.”

Experts say that companies using AI to set or alter pricing could exacerbate the country’s affordability crisis and make it harder for Americans to bear everyday costs. So far this year, at least 90 pieces of legislation have been filed across the country to push back against algorithmic price-fixing, according to Lindsay Owens, the head of the left-leaning thinktank Groundwork Collaborative, who recently authored a book on the topic.

McDonald’s acquired an AI company, Dynamic Yield, in 2019, but has firmly denied using AI in setting menu prices. In a statement released on 1 October, the day before the lawsuit was filed, the chain denied using dynamic pricing and described its pricing tool as simply providing information that franchises are free to decide whether to adopt.

The fast-food chain has been scrutinized over recent years for its elevated prices, and went viral in 2023 over an $18 Big Mac meal at a Connecticut McDonald’s. The franchise’s owner filed a lawsuit alleging that it was the AI pricing tool that suggested the $18 price to the franchise.

According to a fact sheet the chain published in 2024, the average price of a McDonald’s menu item increased about 40% between 2019 and 2024.

fullText:
Wife of Jamaica-born sociologist says project celebrates ‘incredible contributions’ he made to Britain’s culture

Whether it was Thatcherism, populism or the story of the Sony Walkman, Stuart Hall was a public intellectual famed for defining the times. Now a major digital archive of his previously unpublished papers, notebooks, recordings and videos has been launched.

The Jamaica-born sociologist and seminal figure in postwar Black British history died in 2014 aged 82, with his obituary in the Guardian saying he was “among the first to identify key questions of the age”. Hall coined the term Thatcherism and in 1985 warned of the dangers of “authoritarian populism”.

The University of Birmingham, where Hall developed the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, has digitised and released more than 3,100 items donated by his widow, the historian Catherine Hall.

They include notebooks, index cards, his abandoned doctoral thesis and hours of previously inaccessible audio and video tracing the evolution of cultural studies, all within an interactive database.

Also released are his “Origins of the new left” lecture, notebooks on “race and moral panics”, and Encoding/Decoding Cybernetics, a research project exploring Hall’s impact on the architecture of large language models.

The Cadbury Research Library, which has catalogued the original papers, has run the digital archive through a programme that “poisons the data” for bots.

The project lead, Dr Rebecca Roach, working with Helen Fisher and Dr Katherine Parson, said they not create the archive “just for AI to scrape” and commercialise. She said the platform was built to ensure “it doesn’t replicate the exploitation of people of colour and their cultural heritage that technology has historically enabled.”

“One of the things that was really central to us developing the Stuart Hall digital site was to think about what can we learn from Hall’s ideas – and how can we apply that to our current moment with machine learning?,” Roach said.

In response to the era of artificial intelligence, and the questions it raises about culture, copyright and corporate power, the academics behind the Stuart Hall Archive Project have barred AI bots from accessing the data.

Hall died before the AI era fully arrived, but left a body of work with which to interpret it. His theory of representation – examining how media builds meaning through language, symbols and cultural codes – remains relevant amid concerns about algorithmic bias. Doing Cultural Studies, a textbook he co-authored, used the Walkman as a case study of how social, cultural and economic life can be expressed through a single technology.

Roach said it was important to celebrate Black British intellectuals who had made “incredible contributions” to British culture, and noted that while scholars had sometimes been “a bit sniffy” about popular culture, Hall was at its forefront. She called him “a guiding figure for making the world better”.

Alongside the archive, Roach has produced learning materials for primary schoolchildren, while the art collective Vivid Projects has made a zine called Dear Stuart.

University of Birmingham students have also created Walking with Hall, a virtual tour of campus landmarks, raising questions about what it meant for the academic to walk in the shadow of Joseph Chamberlain, the imperialist statesman who founded the university.

Classically educated in Jamaica, Hall came to Britain in 1951 on a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, became the founding editor of New Left Review, and worked as a supply teacher in Brixton before pursuing his academic career.

He met Catherine on an anti-nuclear march in 1963; they moved to Birmingham, where their two children were born and where he made his university department a beacon for debate on media, race, politics, Marxism and critical theory.

From 1997 to 2000 he served on the Runnymede Trust’s commission on the future of multi-ethnic Britain, going on to collaborate with young artists and film-makers, and in 2005 was made a fellow of the British Academy.

Calling the archive “an extraordinary resource”, Prof Daniel McNeil, the Stuart Hall interdisciplinary chair at Birmingham University, said Hall “transformed how we think about culture, identity, power and belonging”.

title: IMF chief urges governments to tighten belts as global debt levels soar
description: Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit...
fullText:
Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit budgets

The head of the International Monetary Fund has called on governments across big economies to tighten their belts as soaring bond yields hit budgets.

Speaking in Singapore, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said global debt-to-GDP ratios were at their highest level since the second world war and on course to hit 100% in the coming years.

She said governments could not rely on rapid economic growth to lift the burden of debt – and instead would have to make “very tough political choices”.

Georgieva was speaking before the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, which are to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them.

“And yet we don’t see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures,” she said.

Bond yields – effectively the interest rate on the debt – have jumped in recent weeks, raising the cost of borrowing for many governments to multi-decade highs as markets adjust to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the war in the Middle East.

“Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defence,” Georgieva said, calling for “an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses”.

The Bulgarian economist suggested central banks should be prepared to raise interest rates to see off resurgent inflation.

The ECB, US Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan have already tightened policy in the face of rising inflation – moves Georgieva said were “highly appropriate” – but the Bank of England has so far left rates on hold at 3.75%.

“Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy,” Georgieva said, suggesting central banks might want to err on the side of caution.

She also stressed the importance of tackling some of the risks of AI, which has buoyed the US stock market but raised fears of mass layoffs.

She highlighted IMF research predicting that the adoption of AI could add half a percentage point to global economic growth if carried out effectively. However, she urged policymakers to “help manage AI’s substantial perils, including large-scale labour market fallout, serious cyber and stability risks and frontier models threatening to escape human control and run amok”.

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who is also chair of the Financial Stability Forum that brings together the world’s central banks, recently warned of the “real and significant” risks posed by frontier AI models and called for the “right to intervene”.

In the UK the chancellor, John Healey, has said he will stick with his predecessor Rachel Reeves’s plans to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – borrowing only to invest – and bring the debt-to-GDP ratio down over time.

fullText:
Commissioner says Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the smartglasses, failed to respond to her inquiries

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Australian privacy regulator has opened an investigation into the China-based software company behind the HeyCyan app in Kmart’s $89 smartglasses, following public outrage over the covert use of the devices.

In August, Guardian Australia reported Kmart had sold out of the Anko-branded discount version of Meta’s smartglasses that can capture images and record high-definition video, which led to widespread concern and calls to ban or restrict their use.

The glasses were removed from Kmart’s website as of Wednesday. The retailer has been approached for comment.

A GetUp petition has had more than 55,000 signatures calling to restrict the use of what has been labelled as “pervert glasses”, and councils around the country have looked to ban the glasses in public spaces such as swimming pools. The federal government is also considering a restriction on use in government workplaces.

The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, was asked by the attorney general to assess the privacy implications of the glasses at the time.

Kind wrote to Kmart and BDI Technology, retailers for the glasses, as well as Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the glasses. She also wrote to Meta – for its Ray-Bans glasses – and Google which is planning its own smartglasses.

In a blog post on Wednesday, Kind announced an investigation has been opened into Shenzhen Qingcheng after it failed to respond to inquiries, “as well as concerns arising from third party analysis of the technology itself as well as the entity’s privacy policy”

None of the other companies will be investigated as part of this process, Kind said.

The privacy commissioner also highlighted the difficulty in applying privacy law to individuals who may use the devices given the privacy act only applies to companies and Commonwealth agencies – not individuals.

“Retailers that sell smart glasses – for example on an e-commerce website – or companies that manufacture them, may not have any Privacy Act obligations if they do not collect any personal information with respect to those devices,” Kind said.

“Instead, the entity providing the software at use in the device is likely to be the entity that collects and holds the information for the purpose of privacy law.”

Kind said that potential changes to the privacy act proposed by the government would strengthen how privacy law would apply to surveillance wearables such as smartglasses.

“The most substantial change will be the replacement of the ‘reasonably necessary for an entity’s functions and activities’ test with a ‘fair and reasonable’ test,” she said.

“The new test will require an entity to look at a range of factors, including the extent to which an individual had genuine choice in the collection of their personal information, as well as the best interests of the child where children are involved.”

Kind said she hoped the community would “find comfort” in the proposed reforms as it would raise the bar over what personal information smartglasses can collect.

“These reforms are likely to become increasingly necessary as we face subsequent generations of surveillance wearables and connected devices, from personal assistant gadgets to ambient recording badges.”

Researchers at the University of Sydney in August analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”.

In a subset of these videos, about 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage.

Canterbury-Bankstown and Sydney City are among the councils in Sydney to have banned the glasses from some venues, as well as Brisbane in Queensland, and Yarra city council in Melbourne.

Shenzhen Qingcheng was approached for comment.

fullText:
‘Techno-optimism’ may lead to reliance on unproven solutions at expense of societal changes needed

Scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action on the issue, according to a study.

The report from the London School of Economics found they are 23% less likelyto sign petitions or take part in protests than peers who doubt that technology is the answer. They are also 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, from reducing flights to changing to a vegan or vegetarian diet.

Fabian Dablander, the lead author, said the belief that technology will largely solve climate change and its consequences, labelled “techno-optimism”, can lead to an over reliance on unproven solutions at the expense of the far-reaching socioeconomic transformations needed to address the climate and nature crisis.

“Technological solutions are often politically attractive because they promise to address climate change without requiring changes to how people live and consume,” said Dablander.

“Strikingly, we see the same tendency at the individual level, with greater faith in technological solutions going hand in hand with less engagement in climate action. Yet technology cannot substitute for the broader societal changes and large-scale shifts in consumption that are also needed.”

The study surveyed more than 9,000 scientists across 115 countries. Overall 27% said they agreed with the statement “technology will largely solve the problems caused by climate change” and 44% disagreed (29% neither agreed nor disagreed).

The “techno-optimist” scientists reported engaging in less civic actions and protests, signed fewer petitions and engaged in less advocacy. They were also less likely to reduce the number of flights they took, cut their car usage or follow a mostly vegan or vegetarian diet.

The report, published in Environmental Research Letters, also found that techno-optimism was most prevalent among scientists with right leaning political views and those working in applied and natural sciences.

Prof Kevin Anderson, one of the world’s leading climate scientists, of the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research at the University of Manchester, who was not involved in the study, said in his experience “a significant proportion of climate academics who enjoy very high incomes from their work, particularly when those incomes are accompanied by prestige, status and glittering honours, have enthusiastically swallowed the blue pill”.

“It offers a convenient escape from any uncomfortable sense of personal responsibility, allowing them to maintain the comforting fiction that they are deeply concerned about the world their children will inherit while continuing to live lives that contribute disproportionately to the problem.”

He added the “accompanying faith in future technological salvation provides another crutch: a way of postponing difficult choices today by placing hope in solutions that may arrive tomorrow”.

“Yet strikingly often, the evidential basis for these promises falls far short of the standards of scrutiny they would demand of research conducted by others. The result is a remarkable inversion of scientific practice: the more uncomfortable the implications of the evidence, the greater the enthusiasm for believing in a future that the evidence does not support.”

fullText:
Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments

Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in Finland after failing to do the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites.

The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajanni are part of a €13bn (£11bn) project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure.

It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representing Google, had felled 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment (EIA).

In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land.

The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres.

On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation.

The EIA is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said.

Tommi Muilu, the head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.”

If Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine.

In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”.

The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.”

Tapani Veistola, the chief operating officer at the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appeared to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, was “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.”

One of the reasons behind it, he said, was the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities.

“The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.”

South Africa's three-city proposal to stage 2036 Olympics
description: The International Olympic Committee confirms South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics.
fullText:
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics in 2036.

Hungary, India, Qatar and Turkey are also working towards becoming first-time hosts, while Germany and South Korea are in discussions with the IOC having held previous summer Games.

The IOC stated that the seven countries are engaged in "continuous dialogue" with the governing body and have set a deadline of 31 October for submissions of stated interest.

Virtual presentations will be given by interested parties to the body's future host commission in November, with IOC feasibility assessments to be carried out by March 2027.

After that, the national Olympic committees, all of whom have previously announced an intention to explore hosting bids, will enter strategic dialogue with the IOC.

The South Africa proposal involves hosting between three cities - Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg.

Durban had been set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2022, but withdrew in 2017.

Ahmedabad, which will welcome the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has bid for the 2038 Asian Games, will be the host city in India's bid.

The city has also staged four of the last five finals in cricket's Indian Premier League at its Narendra Modi stadium, which is reported to have a capacity of 132,000 and is named after the current prime minister of India, who hails from the city.

Budapest and Doha, the capital cities of Hungary and Qatar respectively, are the hosts in their country's bids.

Qatar hosted football's 2022 World Cup, with multiple stadia in the capital, while Budapest has staged the 2022 World Aquatics Championships and 2023 World Athletics Championships.

Istanbul is the nominated city in Turkey's bid, having previously bid unsuccessfully for the 2000, 2008 and 2020 Games.

The largest city in Turkey will host the 2027 European Games.

Germany has hosted the Olympics in 1936 and 1972, in Berlin and Munich respectively, while the latter city is bidding again for 2036.

Meanwhile South Korea capital Seoul, which hosted the Games in 1988, is part of a bid that also involves the province of North Jeolla.

The IOC also confirmed that a number of national Olympic committees are taking part in non-committal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036.

The UK government said in May that it is in "discussions about supporting potential bids" for the Olympics and Paralympics in the 2040s.

The 2028 Games will be held in Los Angeles, while Australia will host the Olympics for the first time in 32 years when Brisbane stages the event in 2032.

title: Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?
description: BBC Sport NI's Andy Gray sits down with Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle to discuss his long career before his biggest managerial test in the World Cup play-offs.
fullText:
As Michael McArdle sits down for an interview with BBC Sport at Windsor Park, he cuts a relaxed figure.

The Scot had just announced his squad for the World Cup play-off with Portugal, for what will be the biggest game of his managerial career to date.

McArdle has only been in the Northern Ireland hot seat since March, when he was announced as Tanya Oxtoby's permanent successor, but has more than 25 years of experience working in football.

There's a clear passion for what he is doing, as he balances the reality of playing one of Europe's top-ranked sides with the dreams of reaching a first World Cup just months into his new role.

But there is one word that keeps cropping up across various topics - family.

McArdle, 48, was born and bred in Moodiesburn to the east of Glasgow, and still lives there to this day.

He met his wife, Tammy, in the village when they were both on the same paper round at the age of 12, and they have now been married for 28 years.

He has three children, Connor, Mya and Cole, and is about to become a grandad for the first time. It's clear how much his family means to him.

But when he talks about family, it's not just in terms of his own life. It is an embodiment of what he is trying to achieve with Northern Ireland.

"Family's crucial to me. We're all a family when we represent the country," he said.

"That's a family of players and a family of staff, but also as an ecosystem and domestic game.

"We're all the one family when we're together and that's a message that will always be strong while I'm at the helm."

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

If Northern Ireland are to make it to their first World Cup in Brazil then there are a number of hurdles they will need to clear.

It would perhaps surpass even the fairytale of qualifying for Euro 2022, when Kenny Shiels led a squad largely made up of amateur players to the promised land.

A change in format has made replicating that feat more difficult, and if Northern Ireland can beat Portugal over two legs then they will face Croatia or, more likely, Iceland.

The Portuguese and Iceland have beaten Northern Ireland over the past two years or so - both quite convincingly.

Even if McArdle's young squad can defy the odds, they will likely face an additional inter-continental play-off in February due to their rankings. It's a tall order.

But that does not stop McArdle and Northern Ireland from dreaming. If anything, it is to be encouraged.

"I think the dream piece is crucial, so we've dreamed about how we get there and what it'll feel like when we do it.

"The other piece of it is the reality. We know it's a highly challenging task first of all to get through Portugal."

McArdle talks about moments within matches, and working with his staff to plan for in-game scenarios.

There's also the excitement that comes with such a big match, and McArdle admits he is "loving" his time in charge.

"You look forward to every game but it's one of those ties that gives you the opportunity to test yourself at the highest level.

"Also the excitement of possibly achieving something and punching above our weight, which we're special at doing."

In his career in football, McArdle has held a number of coaching, academy and development positions.

Before he joined Northern Ireland, he was head of elite women's football at the Scottish FA, and also had a brief interim spell in charge of their senior team.

While the belief is there, McArdle knows he is working on something longer-term, and that can be seen in the make-up of a young squad, which has been hit by a number of injuries to senior players.

While his first two international windows came in quick succession, with two victories over Malta followed by losses to Turkey and Switzerland, the summer has allowed him to spend time around the Women's Premiership in Northern Ireland, building relationships with players and those working in the league.

"I was still getting to know them as people, not as footballers, so that was really important for me to build those relationships.

"Not just the players, either. Getting to know the head coaches a bit more and some of the clubs at boardroom level, to understand how can I serve them and help the club evolution, the domestic league and pathways as well."

While captain Simone Magill is a big loss for the play-offs, she will be with the group for the camp as she builds towards a return to action and provide experience to what is a young group of players.

Not only that, but she will have her newborn daughter, Skye, with her for the duration. McArdle says having those moments are "special".

"Having Simone, Mark and Skye on camp is great. First of all for Simone and Mark to experience what the future is like when Simone's representing Northern Ireland.

"It gives us that window of opportunity and it's something we've planned together over the summer months.

"I think that's crucial because it's one thing knowing the players and the girls that represent us, but also the families that support them as well.

"I'm very passionate about that and I don't underestimate the power of it."

Given the themes throughout, it's no surprise what drives McArdle.

He grew up idolising the likes of Kenny Dalglish, who once was a loan player from Celtic at Cumbernauld United juniors near where he grew up.

His coaching influences are close to home too, and he cites Michael O'Halloran, a youth coach in Glasgow, and Sir Alex Ferguson, who was a "god" coming from the east end of the city.

Further afield, the likes of Arrigo Sacchi - whose AC Milan side he used to watch on VHS in the 90s - Jose Mourinho and Rafa Benitez have all factored into his thinking.

"What drew me towards Sacchi, Mourinho and Benitez was not just the tactical side of the game, but how they managed it and their leadership.

"They didn't play professionally and it kind of aligned with myself, although I didn't realise at the time."

But it's in Moodiesburn where his DNA is, and it is the values he learned there that have shaped him into the coach he is today.

"Growing up in the village and growing up as a family I was always going to care for people and be in a service role.

"It was always going to be my calling. I'm just blessed that football has given me the opportunity to develop a knowledge and skill set to work at the highest level of an industry."

McArdle's passion for football is clear, but family also plays a role in helping him escape the demands of the job.

He goes to the theatre with his daughter, Mya, or to the cinema or concerts with Tammy.

A sports fan, he also goes and watches his sons play football, without the stresses of management and coaching.

"Representing my family is everything to me.

"We've stayed in the same village all our lives. You represent the village as well and that becomes a big piece of what we do.

"So those aspects of family fuel you."

title: Republic of Ireland boss Ward focused on World Cup amid Villa link
description: Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward says that "nothing is tempting" her away from her job as they prepare for a World Cup qualifying double-header against Kazakhstan.
fullText:
Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward says that her focus is on reaching the Women's World Cup amid speculation linking her to a move back to the Women's Super League.

The Republic have a chance to book a spot at next summer's finals in Brazil when they face a play-off against Kazakhstan before, if they progress, a two-legged final against either Belgium or Poland.

Ward, who replaced Eileen Gleeson in January 2025, has been linked with the vacant post at her former club Aston Villa. However, she insists leading the Republic of Ireland to the World Cup is her primary ambition.

"Nothing is tempting when I'm in this job, you know I love this job and I love working here," Ward said.

"I don't think anything can take my attention away from these next four games so it's not a conversation and it's not anything I would entertain.

"My heart and my focus, I came here to try and get to a World Cup and that's all I'm going to think about for the next four games."

The Republic of Ireland made history when they qualified for the World Cup in 2023 for the first time ever. However, they were unable to progress from the group, beaten by co-hosts Australia and Canada, before drawing with Nigeria.

Three years on, Ward now has the chance to lead the team back to the biggest stage in international football.

"You've seen how I've spoken in the last two years and with immense pride in this job," she continued.

"I'm here because I want to get to a World Cup and I think we've made tremendous strides and steps as a nation, and it would be the cherry on the cake, but, look we've got four games, four cup finals.

"We have to give everything, blood, sweat and tears. We have to leave everything out there in everything we do and if we do that, we've got every chance."

The two-legged tie against Kazakhstan begins with a trip to the Astana Arena on Friday, 9 October (12:00 BST) before the return fixture in Cork four days later.

The Republic of Ireland are unbeaten at Pairc Ui Chaoimh, but Ward is taking nothing for granted against a Kazakhstan side ranked 98th in the world.

"We have to go up another level, we have to make sure that we're performing, and we're focused at the highest level.

"If we do that then we'll get the job done. We've got an unbelievable squad that are hugely talented and they will look after each other.

"I think anyone that comes in that will know their role I think we're really clear with what we do, what we want and how we play."

Ward will have to make changes, with captain Katie McCabe and Marissa Sheva both suspended for the first leg, while the experienced Denise O'Sullivan is also unavailable.

Tara O'Hanlon is out with a hamstring injury and Saoirse Noonan has also been ruled out of both games with an ankle problem.

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft has been called into the squad for the first time.

Despite the absence of multiple key leaders, Ward says this is a chance for others to shine.

"No matter who plays, naturally when you take the likes of Katie and Denise out of your team, they're two big leaders but that's an opportunity for players to step up.

"Katie's here for a reason, she's got a big part to play off the pitch, and she will and she'll lead the group as she normally does.

"Then it'll be over to those that go out there and I have full belief in every single one of this group to go and get the job done."

title: South Korea to review military service exemption after Asian Games row
description: South Korea are discussing making changes to military exemptions for athletes after Asian Games controversy.
fullText:
South Korea's government says it intends to review the military exemptions it grants athletes after the controversy surrounding South Korean footballers at the Asian Games.

Following their win against hosts Japan in the final, three players were criticised for celebrating securing their exemptions, including South Korea captain Lee Gi-hyuk.

South Korean men are required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of active military service before the age of 28.

Lee apologised for his remarks, but Culture, Sports and Tourism minister Choi Hwi-young says he will "review" the exemption.

Choi called Lee's comments "utterly immature" and said the system, which has been in place for more than 50 years, "will inevitably have to be scaled back".

South Korean captain Lee sparked outrage in his home country when he held up his gold medal and triumphantly announced he was "not going to the military".

The government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.

"It is true that the system has contributed to helping outstanding artists and athletes maintain and develop their abilities," Choi said at a National Assembly Culture, Sports and Tourism Committee hearing.

Captain apologises for gloating over military service exemption

'Grateful, proud and at peace' - emotional Messi plays final Argentina game

"However, the values attached to fairness and public perceptions of military service have changed. I agree that the system should be comprehensively reviewed once again."

Cho Kye-won, a member of the Democratic Party of Korea, questioned Choi on the topic and said the incident "left young people with a serious sense of unfairness".

The current system grants exemptions only to Olympic medallists finishing third or better and to Asian Games gold medallists, and more than 80% of those benefits are concentrated in the Asian Games.

He suggested winning a world championship in any sport is harder than winning the Asian Games, yet world champions in other sports receive no service benefit.

"Of the 44 people who qualified for the benefit at this Asian Games, 36 were in soccer and baseball," Cho said.

title: 'Bring the magic' - Scotland's Ross eyes World Cup dream
description: Scotland assistant coach Leanne Ross never played at a World Cup but thinks the current squad has what it takes to get through the play-offs for Brazil 2027.
fullText:
Leanne Ross is Scotland's most decorated player, earning 133 international caps across a career which garnered 14 league titles and 13 major cup medals, but still the national team's assistant coach wants more.

Having reached the 2017 European Championship, Ross was part of the first women's squad to compete at a major tournament, but one thing has eluded her. A World Cup.

Ross retired after the Euros, meaning she did not take part in the 2019 edition in France, but her dream has not been dashed.

Scotland are a wee bit away from booking flights and hotels for Brazil 2027. Up next is a round one play-off double-header against Czech Republic, live on the BBC, but the excitement is building.

"It would be huge," Ross said the day before the Scots travel to Pardubice, east of Prague, for the first leg. "I never got to do it as a player, reaching that World Cup stage.

"I played in the Euro finals and that was an amazing experience and just topped off my career as a player, but to go and do it as part of the coaching staff, it would be such a proud moment."

Scots recall 'versatile' Kerr & Thomas for World Cup play-offs

Ross is part of the SWNT furniture, having seamlessly shifted into a coaching role following her stellar playing career, so she knows a thing or two about what makes the team tick.

She also knows what its like to taste play-off pain.

Two years ago, it was Finland who denied Scotland a place at the 2025 Euros. Before that, Republic of Ireland romped to the World Cup in Australia.

Many in the squad still carry the scars of both final-hurdle failures.

From the outside, it's fair to fear a repeat, with heavyweights Sweden potentially lying in wait in round two.

But Ross isn't thinking like that. Instead, her confidence of "getting back to where we want to be" stems from the squad bringing their "magic".

"The progress that we're making and the way that we're playing at this moment is a real good opportunity for us to do that," Ross - who is Glasgow City head coach - said of ending the team's eight-year wait for a return to a major tournament.

"You look at the quality we have, the teams that they're playing for, the environments that they're in and individually them bringing their magic into this team and putting that all together.

"I think it's a really exciting time for Scotland with the players we have. We need to make sure we give them the platform to go, play and get themselves on that world stage."

title: Leicester hooker Theobald-Thomas forced to retire
description: Leicester Tigers announce hooker Finn Theobald-Thomas retire immediately on medical grounds.
fullText:
Leicester Tigers hooker Finn Theobald-Thomas has been forced to retire immediately on medical grounds.

The 23-year-old joined Tigers ahead of the 2023-24 season and made 33 appearances.

The Prem club did not disclose the nature of Theobald-Thomas's injury, but said, external that they and the Rugby Players' Association will "continue to support Finn as he begins the transition into retirement".

"It's difficult to put into words what rugby has meant to me," Theobald-Thomas wrote on Instagram., external

"This isn't how I imagined my career ending, and having something I've worked towards and loved for so much of my life taken out of my hands is incredibly difficult to accept.

"But when I look back, a kid from Bradmore lived the dream of playing for his boy hood rugby club, I feel nothing but pride and gratitude. Rugby has given me some of the best moments of my life, friendships that will last forever, and memories I'll carry with me long after I've stopped playing."

Tigers head coach Geoff Parling said: "I'm gutted with this news of Finn's retirement from rugby, both from a team point of view and for him personally to have such a promising rugby journey cut short."

"He is a loveable bloke who is exactly the type of character you'd want to be around, unselfish and fully invested in the team. We'll miss him and he knows that he'll always be part of this team."

title: Former UFC security guard Everett wins fighter contract
description: Former UFC employee Sal Everett wins a fighter contract with the promotion after knocking out Ozzy Martin in Dana White's Contender Series.
fullText:
Just a few months ago, Sal Everett was working for the UFC as a security guard and runner - now he's earned a contract to fight for the promotion.

In Dana White's Contender Series, the 29-year-old knocked out fellow American Ozzy Martin with a devastating combination in the first round.

UFC president White awarded Everett a contract with the promotion after the victory, before admitting he struggled to contain his excitement after watching him win.

"That's why I got up and walked out after he won, I don't want to be overly celebrating," said White.

"Sal is one of the greatest kids ever and it couldn't happen to a better person - I'm happy for him.

"I think this contract changes his life so he doesn't have to work at the office."

Everett joined the UFC about three years ago as a security guard, before later becoming a runner for White, doing errands.

Everett trained in MMA while working for the UFC and won the first four fights of his career before being offered a spot in the Contender Series.

He recently left his job at the UFC so he could focus on his career as a professional fighter.

"Hey boss, I'm ready to be in the UFC," Everett said during his post-fight interview.

"The whole division, you know my name. I'm not backing down from any challenges."

Everett's win comes one week after Briton George Staines' victory, where he won a UFC contract after stopping Loai Abushaar inside 61 seconds.

title: Inside Scarlets and their struggle for existence
description: Scarlets are ready to fight for their existence as the Welsh Rugby Union presses on with controversial plans to cut a west Wales club.
fullText:
You pass the first reminder of Llanelli's rugby identity before you even reach the town.

In Felinfoel stands a statue of Phil Bennett, captain of the Llanelli team which famously beat New Zealand in 1972.

A few miles further on, Welsh Sports Hall of Fame inductee Ray Gravell is immortalised outside Parc y Scarlets.

There are no footballers or cricketers competing for space here. The sporting story being told is overwhelmingly one of rugby.

Which makes the question hanging over the place particularly brutal: what happens if professional rugby disappears from Llanelli?

The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) plans to cut its professional men's teams from four to three. Under its preferred model, Scarlets or Ospreys will cease to exist by 2028.

WRU sticking to three-team plan - Reddin

WRU seek to sell SRC side RGC to private investors

Inside Parc y Scarlets, photographs of former teams and famous victories cover the walls.

Rugby autobiographies fill a bookshelf in the cafe, where today's lunch for the players is roast beef.

The former Wales and British and Irish Lions scrum-half is back coaching at the club where he began his career. His grandfather was once a physio here, running on with the magic sponge for Gravell.

Now Peel talks about the school run and his son playing junior rugby.

It is a theme that keeps returning during a day at Parc y Scarlets with the Scrum V Podcast.

Director of rugby Nigel Davies grew up in Trimsaran, a few miles away. Peel is from nearby Tumble. A large proportion of the current squad grew up playing rugby in the towns and villages Scarlets represent.

Even managing director Jon Daniels once played for nearby Llangennech.

He believes that connection is precisely what is at stake.

"We don't have Premier League or Championship football teams," he said.

"When they want to play sport, they still play rugby in the (school) yards in west Wales."

Later, his language becomes starker.

"I genuinely fear for west Wales if this continues the way it is," Daniels said. "For the young generations of Wales, I think there would be a real loss."

It is the emotional heart of Scarlets' argument for survival.

The problem is that Welsh rugby's current predicament cannot be solved by emotion alone.

The WRU holds most of the cards.

Scarlets can make their case, but cannot guarantee their own future.

Daniels argues Welsh rugby should be asking how it can preserve four teams rather than accepting one must disappear.

"We have not seen the numbers laid down in front of us to prove that we can't sustain four," he says.

But that raises an obvious question in return: where are Scarlets' numbers?

Daniels says season-ticket revenue is ahead of last year, attendances increased by 7% last season, sponsorship is performing well and the stadium is generating money away from matchdays.

But when pressed on where the additional money needed to sustain four properly funded teams would come from, there is no clear answer.

"Can we put together a 10-year plan where, in 10 years' time, we can have four competitive, successful, viable teams?" he asks.

It is an argument for more time but not yet a funded alternative, and Scarlets do not control the timetable.

On one of the cafe walls, among black-and-white photographs and faded old jerseys, is an image that looks strikingly modern.

The colours are sharp, the picture unmistakably digital. It shows Scarlets celebrating their 2017 league title - the last time a Welsh team won the competition.

James 'Cubby' Davies played in that team. Now he helps recruit the next generation.

He says the "secret sauce" was connection.

"We built success on the pitch through a lot of the things that we did off the pitch," he said. "We just connected as a group."

Now his job is to build another.

Davies says that uncertainty over Welsh rugby's future meant Scarlets were late entering the recruitment market last season.

There is another meeting with the WRU on the day we visit.

Davies talks about planning ahead, then hesitates.

"We're very hopeful of our... what's the word? Our existence, obviously," he said.

A strange word to hear in the everyday surroundings of a professional sports club.

On the other side of the stadium, past a couple of burger vans with their shutters still down, around 40 players are playing football in an indoor training barn.

There is shouting, laughter and arguing over decisions.

After two opening defeats and plenty of analysis, director Davies wants people smiling again.

"It's all about bringing the energy," he says.

It is striking to watch at a club whose very existence is being debated.

Daniels calls the constant speculation around Welsh rugby the "jungle drums".

"Sometimes the potential impact on human beings is lost in all that," he said.

Players train. Coaches prepare. Contracts are considered. Lunch is served.

This is what uncertainty looks like inside a sports club.

Mostly, it looks surprisingly normal.

Nine miles away, another club can make its own case.

Six Ospreys were selected for the 2013 British and Irish Lions tour - twice as many as the whole of Scotland. Only two Welshmen made the Lions squad in 2025.

Ospreys are planning for the future too, with St Helen's in Swansea being redeveloped as their new home.

Llanelli's built-up area has about 42,000 people and Swansea's around 170,000. Dublin city alone has almost 600,000. Johannesburg has millions.

It helps explain the WRU's logic.

On a map, consolidation can look obvious. On the ground, Scarlets and Ospreys have different histories, communities and identities.

For now, Daniels refuses to accept the choice and urges caution.

"We should do that before we just jump to 'right, we cut two teams', or now 'we cut one team'," he says.

But if the WRU presses ahead with three, Scarlets and Ospreys will eventually have to make a different argument.

Not simply why they should survive, why they should survive instead of the other.

Players drift back into the cafe. Plates of roast beef appear beneath photographs of those who came before them.

For now, Scarlets continue with the strangely ordinary business of running a professional rugby club while waiting to discover whether they will remain one.

title: Are Man City equipped for dual demands this time?
description: Manchester City have had a strong start to the WSL season, but have they showed they are capable of juggling Champions League football?
fullText:
When Manchester City began the defence of their Women's Super League title there was one question on everyone's minds.

Can they compete on multiple fronts?

In previous years, City have struggled to go far in the Women's Champions League at the same time as challenging for the WSL title.

They made just three signings in the summer and retained most of their squad from last season when they won a first WSL title in a decade.

Manager Andree Jeglertz would have to rotate his squad and live up to expectations - and so far he has done a good job.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

It has been an impressive start to the season for City, who have won every game in the WSL and are yet to lose in Europe.

Their squad depth has been important, as Jeglertz is yet to name the same starting XI, but it has not impacted their rhythm.

And his substitutions have had an impact with Beth Mead assisting against Birmingham City and Kerstin Casparij scoring with her first touch against Arsenal.

City also came from 2-0 down at Bayern Munich to draw their opening Champions League game and also came from behind to level 1-1 with Real Madrid.

They have also gained six points from losing positions in the WSL, the most by any team.

It remains early days but is Jeglertz showing he can juggle competing demands well?

"If you look at all the games we have played this season so far, I think the substitutions and changes we have made in the last half an hour has quite often turned the game around," said Jeglertz following their 4-2 win over Arsenal.

"We really have finished off on a high. We have never dropped that. I think that is something for us to [take forward].

"You can only start with 11 players but you can make five substitutions. The ones that have come in, no matter who it is, have always affected it in a good way."

Despite finishing runners-up to Chelsea in the WSL in both 2019 and 2020, City did not go beyond the last-16 stage in Europe during those seasons.

They came second in the WSL again in 2021 and reached at least the quarter-finals in both domestic cup competitions and the Champions League.

But that took its toll on them the following two years as they fell in the qualifying stages of the Champions League and dropped to third, then fourth in the WSL.

They do not want to repeat it again.

England international Lauren Hemp, who has been in electric form, said their draws in Europe were "not our standard" despite facing tough opposition.

Manager Jeglertz was pleased with their second half display against Real Madrid but like Hemp, still craves more as he knows the challenge will only get harder.

"We have played two teams that are definitely at a very high level. If you want to go far in the tournament, you also need to win these games," said Jeglertz.

"We have two points and haven't lost and we had two good halves. But we're still looking for a 90 minutes where we feel we can do a great game.

"It's an OK start. It's not ideal but it's a good start. We know what is needed from us for the rest of the tournament."

City know there is a long way to go. It is only five games into the WSL season and they have another four matches to play in the league phase in Europe.

Several players including Vivianne Miedema, Sydney Lohmann, Rebecca Knaak and Risa Shimizu are recovering from injury, while Sam Coffey picked up a knock in their crucial victory over Arsenal on Sunday.

But they have already showed their squad depth is good enough and they have resilience which will be needed later down the line.

Of their 16 goals scored in the WSL this season, 10 have come in the second half, including three in stoppage time.

Key players such as Kerstin Casparij, Khadija Shaw and Yui Hasegawa have all played fewer minutes at this stage than they did last season in the WSL.

USA international Coffey, one of their most crucial midfielders, has featured in every game but has only played 90 minutes once as Jeglertz has rotated effectively.

This was shown on Sunday as vice-captain Casparij came on against Arsenal to give her side the lead in the 63rd minute.

"At half-time I knew I was going to come on so I had a good chunk of time to prepare and get ready to play my game," said Casparij.

"That's what Andree does. He's really clear with us and it allows me to play my game, trust my instinct, trust my gut and play with a lot of freedom.

"We've got incredible resilience and mentality within this team. We've got incredible players coming off the bench, changing the game.

"That is so important because it's the whole team that you need, especially in a long season like this. Nothing is won yet but we have to keep up this mentality."

title: Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
description: Wada president Witold Banka says Kenya must strengthen testing, investigations and anti-doping enforcement before hosting the 2029 World Athletics Championships.
fullText:
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .

Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.

Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.

"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.

"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."

Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.

The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.

More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.

The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.

"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.

Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships

Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.

For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.

"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."

Another challenge is testing infrastructure.

Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.

Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.

Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.

Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.

The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.

That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.

Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.

"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.

"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."

Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.

"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.

"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."

He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.

According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.

Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

title: Chisora, 42, to fight in December after deciding against retirement
description: Derek Chisora's last fight was billed as his retirement bout, but the 42-year-old says he intends to box in December.
fullText:
Derek Chisora says he is not retiring and will fight again in December.

The 42-year-old Briton lost to Deontay Wilder in April in what was billed as his 50th and final fight.

However, Chisora has since refused to confirm his retirement. Speaking at a news conference on Tuesday, he said he believed he would fight in December against Murat Gassiev.

"December will be me versus Gassiev," Chisora said.

"We're going to decide where, either in London or Manchester. We're going to put two belts on the line, I believe, the IBA and the one Gassiev holds.

"What people have to understand is that what the IBA does is unbelievable. I believe this goes deeper than that we're doing here right now.

"I believe it's going to get better and better. In December we'll be fighting."

Gassiev is the WBA 'super' heavyweight world champion, but his status is unclear after reports claimed Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua would be fighting for his world title in their contest on 11 December.

The Russian said on Tuesday he was unsure if he remained the WBA's world champion.

Chisora's news conference was hosted by the IBA, the body that was stripped of its status as amateur boxing's governing body by the International Olympic Committee in 2023 and has since been staging professional bouts.

Gassiev's recent bouts have been under the IBA's banner and he was upgraded to the WBA's 'super' champion in June after Oleksandr Usyk relinquished the belt.

Several of Chisora's recent bouts have been billed as farewell fights and there have been repeated calls from people within the boxing community for the veteran to retire because of his age.

Chisora has 36 wins in 50 fights and defended his decision to continue fighting.

"I never said I was retired. They [the organisers] said '50 last dance'," he said.

"This is why you've got [films like] Rush Hour 1, Rush Hour 2, Coming to America 1, Coming to America 2. You understand?

"So this is The Last Dance 3. Listen, trust me, I'm a seller, I sell. That's my job."

title: Wrexham's Kop: The project matching the club's rise
description: Wrexham's new Kop stand a signal of their ambition to keep climbing from the Championship to the Premier League.
fullText:
Wrexham's new Kop stand is rising even quicker than the football club's fortunes have soared in recent years.

The £70m development at the Racecourse - the oldest international football ground still in use - has been described as a "real symbol of hope".

The Kop stood derelict and dormant for years, a stark reminder of the troubled times endured by the north Wales club.

But under Hollywood owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac the club are aiming for the Premier League, with the Kop rebuild central to those ambitions.

The stand is scheduled to be fully operational by the start of next season.

The man overseeing the project is Aidan Miller, Wrexham's chief strategy officer.

He is responsible for the long-term development of the Championship club, which only three years ago was playing non-league football.

"The speed at which we've got through the leagues has been incredible," Miller told BBC Sport Wales.

"We are playing catch-up and we're trying to make ourselves ready for the next level.

"We've always gone to the next level from the footballing side before the rest of the club is necessarily ready to.

"Now we're trying to do it a bit more proactively, rather than necessarily just reactively."

The new Kop stand will have 7,500 seats to take the ground's capacity to more than 18,000, the club's application having been officially approved by Wrexham County Borough Council this week.

It will incorporate facilities such as dressing room areas, media provision and hospitality.

In addition to improvements that have already been made, it will make the Racecourse fit for the Premier League - should the team achieve promotion.

Reynolds and Mac completed their takeover of the then National League club, owned by Wrexham Supporters' Trust, in February 2022.

The pair have made no secret of their ambition to see Wrexham in the top flight and have backed manager Phil Parkinson.

The team secured three successive promotions to reach the Championship, then narrowly missed out on the play-offs last season.

But Reynolds and Mac have also supported and championed local community projects and ensured the football club's impact is felt beyond the pitch.

"They've delivered in terms of the optimism, the confidence," Miller said.

"You notice it as soon as you walk around the place - the optimism, the buzz.

"There are people who've worked here that been through thick and thin for several years and you can see that they've got a spring in their step.

"You can see that as you go around the city as well. It's great to see it flooding out of this stadium to other elements."

Why a new stand has become symbolic for Wrexham

FAW eyes more Wales games at Wrexham's Racecourse

Before joining Wrexham, Miller worked for seven years on Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium at Bramley-Moore Dock on the banks of the River Mersey.

"Premier League clubs don't necessarily build new stadiums and they tend to happen in certain intervals," Miller said.

"They're difficult to deliver and therefore when you do deliver them, they're brilliant.

"They're great to see in action, in operation. It's a testament to all the people that go into that.

"That club had a long period of trying to develop a stadium and put various phases to it.

"Eventually we managed to do it. A lot of people put so much into that making that happen and making it work.

"I am really proud of that - it's a brilliant stadium."

If rebuilding the Kop was not enough of a project to get on with, Wrexham have also undertaken work at three other sites.

There has been significant developments at the academy site located at Darland High School in Rossett with the laying of new pitches.

The women's team base at The Rock in Rhosymedre - which the club purchased in 2025 - has seen major upgrades such as a new pitch and gym facilities.

At Colliers Park, a new pavilion for the first team has been built at the complex operated by the Football Association of Wales (FAW).

"They're all important and big developments in their own right," Miller added.

"They're all important from a club perspective in terms of this long-term piece that we're talking about.

"The club wants to be in a position where its academy is reaching improved levels, improved statuses and we get the players coming through that.

"That's what's needed for this club to be sustainable in the long term.

"The owners have been really clear about their appetite to invest in the women's team and how they're going about doing that.

"We bought The Rock just over a year ago, so it is a really important step to continue to refurbish that and make changes to it."

While the aim on the pitch is to reach the Premier League, the new Kop is merely the beginning of the work to further develop the Racecourse.

Having described the new Kop as a "real symbol of hope ahead", chief executive Michael Williamson has said the ground's ideal capacity would be between 26,000 and 29,000.

Wrexham recently announced it had purchased The Turf, the historic pub located next door to the ground, in order to "protect the future of the club" and land which was occupied by the former Dickens Car showroom.

"It's just continuing to take those steps forward," Miller said of the Racecourse's future.

"It's continuing to make it bigger, larger, better and just continuing to improve the experience."

title: Test cricket's biggest scandals - your results revealed
description: See what BBC Sport readers voted as Test cricket's biggest scandals, together with contributions from the TMS team.
fullText:
On Friday, Australia will play their first Test in South Africa since the sandpapergate scandal rocked the cricketing world eight years ago.

To mark one of the biggest controversies the game has ever seen, Test Match Special asked you which is Test cricket's biggest scandal.

Ten of the most notorious scandals in Test cricket were picked out by a TMS panel and readers of the BBC Sport website then ranked them.

The results have been revealed on the TMS podcast by BBC chief cricket commentator Jonathan Agnew, former England fast bowler Steven Finn and TMS scorer Andy Zaltzman.

The full results are below and you can listen to the podcast here.

Pakistan had already lost the series in England in 2006, yet were cruising to victory in the final Test at The Oval. However, Australian umpire Darrel Hair asked for the ball to be changed midway through the afternoon session on the fourth day. Ball-tampering was suggested and Pakistan refused to play after tea. The match was abandoned and years later awarded to England, after some back and forth.

Agnew: "Pakistan weren't accused of ball-tampering, they were found guilty of ball-tampering, on the field, without any opportunity to defend themselves. The rule at the time was if the umpire on the field suspected ball-tampering, the ball was changed and penalty runs were awarded. It didn't feel fair."

Zaltzman: "It ended up with England awarded the Test so therefore they won the series 3-0. It means that whenever we look at the biggest first-innings deficit overturned to win a Test, this game comes out on top - 331 runs. It irritates me slightly."

England's Test match against Pakistan in 1987 was stopped mid-game for more than 24 hours when the tourists' skipper Mike Gatting became embroiled in a row with home umpire Shakoor Rana.

Agnew: "I'm a bit surprised this is so low. The knock-on was England didn't tour Pakistan for many years. England felt they were being stitched up by Pakistani umpires. There was a total lack of trust, going both ways, between England and Pakistan for a very long time."

Zaltzman: "This was before neutral umpires and there was a sense umpiring wasn't quite as fair as it could have been, which all exploded in that moment."

Finn: "It blows my mind that there weren't neutral umpires. My first summer of Test cricket had DRS and neutral umpires."

The third Test in the 1975 Ashes was abandoned when the pitch was vandalised overnight by supporters of George Davis, who had been jailed for armed robbery the previous year. "George Davis is innocent" was written on the wall around Headingley.

Finn: "I can't fathom turning up to a Test match and the pitch - the most sacred, untouchable of places - it's staggering that people managed to do that."

Zaltzman: "It highlights how vulnerable cricket is to this sort of thing. A small bit of the field is damaged and the whole game has to be abandoned."

Agnew: "There was no security. These days, the grounds are locked down. It was set up for an England win, but could have been a really good game of cricket. It's a bizarre story."

When Australia's richest man, Kerry Packer, failed to boost the ratings of his Channel Nine TV network with live cricket, he created his own product: World Series Cricket. The plan was simple - Packer recruited the best players in the world to stage his own matches.

Agnew: "Virtually everything you see about modern cricket can be traced back to World Series. It was incredible, innovative and exciting. I was 18 years old, playing club cricket in Melbourne and captivated by the coverage."

Finn: "There's a similar revolution going on at the moment with T20 leagues allowing players to drift away from Test cricket. The temptation to be involved in something new and exciting would have been very interesting."

Zaltzman: "It was extremely high-calibre cricket, but not even counted in first-class statistics, let alone Test stats. I don't really see it as a scandal at all, it was more cricket growing up. This really modernised the sport."

In the 1994 Lord's Test against South Africa, Michael Atherton was caught by TV cameras rubbing dirt on the ball. Atherton's explanation was that he was trying to maintain the condition of the ball, rather than alter it. Trouble was, he told the match referee he was using the dirt to keep his hands dry.

Agnew: "This was a really tough time. I've thought about this a lot over the years and I'm not sure Michael knew the rules at the time - cricketers often don't. It's OK to rub your hand in the dirt, but you can't put soil on to the ball. It was a huge story. It was everywhere."

Our top five kicks off with the Pakistan spot-fixing scandal of 2010, when no-balls deliberately bowled in the Lord's Test ultimately resulted in three of the tourists' players - team captain Salman Butt and fast bowlers Mohammad Asif and Mohammad Amir - spending time in jail.

Finn: "This was my first summer of Test cricket. It was such a weird atmosphere. We were warming up, looked up to the Pakistan dressing room and there were two officials in suits and blazers reading the News of the World. That was the day we went on to win the game. We didn't celebrate any of the wickets because of what transpired."

Zaltzman: "Amir had burst on to the scene as a teenager - he'd only bowled three no-balls in his previous five Tests. As a cricket fan, one of the deep sadnesses was Amir was one of the best talents to have emerged in years. It was an individual tragedy. A young player had been led astray."

The Australians feature again here, but this time the guilty party was England, who developed a plan of intimidatory fast bowling aimed at the bodies of the hosts' batters in the 1932-33 Ashes series.

Agnew: "For me, this would be bottom. It was an entirely legitimate ploy. They call us whingeing Poms, but the Australians were pretty good at whingeing about the way [Harold] Larwood was bowling."

Finn: "Cricket is a game of small margins. You use the laws and the bandwidth within those laws. Play on, I say."

The most recent of the scandals in our list is Sandpapergate, when Australia's cricketers were found to have used sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during their Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Finn: "I was completely and utterly baffled and shocked that someone thought this was a good idea and they would get away with it. There are so many cameras and you are so acutely aware when you are playing that those cameras have the ability to zoom in. To think you'd be able to pull sandpaper out of your pocket, rub it on the ball and then hide it down your pants is completely unfathomable. I was shocked they had taken altering the state of the ball to that kind of level."

Agnew: "If you're a bowler you want to control what's happening with the ball and you'll see if something has gone on with it. For me, there are some unanswered questions. It was one of the most stupid things ever seen on a cricket field."

A close second in our vote was the Basil D'Oliveira affair of 1968, when England's tour of South Africa was called off over the inclusion in their squad of mixed-race all-rounder D'Oliveira. At the time, South Africa was operating under a system of racial segregation known as apartheid.

Agnew: "You can actually trace this affair all the way up to the birth of a new nation. When you unpick it, look at the consequences, it was eventually the birth of a new South Africa. For me, this would be number one."

Zaltzman: "There's still a lot that is not known about the decision to not pick D'Oliveira in the original England squad. There had been pressure put on him by the English cricketing establishment - the establishment came out very badly from that. It had a huge impact on the world and the gradual dismantling of apartheid."

Top of the list is former South Africa captain Hansie Cronje, who admitted to match-fixing having become involved with Indian bookmakers. Cronje's most infamous plot came in a dead-rubber fifth Test against England at Centurion Park in 2000. The match had been badly affected by rain, but Cronje was adamant the teams should do all they could to ensure it did not end in a draw.

He negotiated with England skipper Nasser Hussain for both teams to forfeit an innings, leaving the tourists with a final-day run-chase, which they completed. England were unaware, but Cronje had engineered a result.

Agnew: "This was unbelievable. It came to light by accident. The Delhi police were trying to tap a phone of a bookmaker and accidentally tapped the phone of Hansie Cronje. Thank goodness they did because hopefully it is now much more difficult for a player to manipulate games of cricket."

Zaltzman: "At the time, we all thought it was good. Cronje's generous deal made a contest on the final day of a dead rubber. Until the true story came out, we didn't realise what had gone was criminal. The shock of the story merits its place in this countdown."

Finn: "A lot of these things have been the catalyst for necessary change in cricket and this was the biggest one."

title: 'Draining' few days for Gauff after online racist abuse
description: Coco Gauff says she had a "draining" few days after receiving racist abuse online before her fourth-round China Open exit.
fullText:
Coco Gauff said she had a "draining" few days after receiving racist abuse online before her fourth-round China Open exit.

The American received an "insane" amount of racist comments and direct messages following an incident in her third-round win over 16-year-old Sun Xinran on Monday.

China's Sun thought she had hit a winner late in the first set, but Gauff raised her hand to halt play because of a flickering light in the side panels surrounding the court.

After a video review - which players are allowed to request - the point was replayed, with Gauff winning it and subsequently going on to clinch the match.

The 22-year-old posted a lengthy statement explaining what had happened and later condemned the racist abuse she received in response.

Gauff was beaten 6-3 6-3 in her next match against Elise Mertens on Wednesday.

Asked how she had felt over the past 36 hours, Gauff said: "It has been kind of draining, I'm not going to lie.

"I just turn off my phone and move on. I mean, there's nothing you can do."

A spokesperson for the Women's Tennis Association said it was appalled by the abuse. It said it was in contact with Gauff "to offer our full support".

A statement given to the news agency AFP said the governing body was "seeking action" against the abusive content.

Gauff, who won the title in Beijing in 2024, committed 34 unforced errors and eight double faults against Mertens.

"I was just a bit flat. That's the main thing," Gauff said.

"The level was there at some points, I just didn't sustain it the whole match."

Belgium's Mertens will play former world number one Iga Swiatek in the quarter-finals after the six-time major champion Swiatek beat American teenager Iva Jovic 6-1 6-3.
